episodes.180899: After a squall line moved through the area on July 18, 2023, another complex of thunderstorms moved through Middle Tennessee early on July 19th. Heavy rain was common with these thunderstorms as they produced three to six inches of rain across the northwest portion of the area. Fortunately, no significant flooding reports were received. Meanwhile, one rogue strong thunderstorm in southern Lawrence County did produce wind damage.
episodes.180932: An upper level disturbance passing over CO combined with sufficient low-level moisture allowed for scattered storms to develop over northeastern NM during the afternoon of July 19th. These scattered storms stayed over very rural areas through the mid-to-late afternoon period likely producing strong winds and large hail. There was only one report of an estimated severe wind gust just east of Gladstone, NM however.
episodes.180967: Historic flash flooding struck parts of far western Kentucky. Among the hardest hit counties was Graves County, which had not completely recovered from a catastrophic tornado in December of 2021. The city of Mayfield, which bore the brunt of the December 2021 tornado, experienced catastrophic flooding that inundated dozens of homes, businesses, schools, and various other institutions. The governor of Kentucky visited the city of Mayfield to tour the damage. Some smaller communities suffered catastrophic damage, such as Arlington in Carlisle County, where multiple homes were flooded. Swiftly moving water through Arlington prompted water rescues from emergency services. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 69 in southwest Graves County, near the community of Wingo. Other high-profile road closures included U.S. Highways 51, 62, and 45 at various locations in Ballard, McCracken, Graves, and Hickman Counties. Numerous water rescues were conducted for people stranded in homes and vehicles. Dozens of roads were washed out in several counties, including Ballard, Carlisle, Hickman, Fulton, and Graves. Swift water was across many roads, and water even overtopped a few bridges, including U.S. 60 between Paducah and Kevil. Crop damage was expected to run into the millions of dollars. At one farm alone in southern Graves County, crop damage was estimated around 40,000 dollars. The downtown area of Fulton was flooded, including at least one business. Widespread street flooding occurred in Murray, and at least one business was sandbagged. About a dozen businesses were flooded in Ballard County, along with another dozen residences. Widespread rainfall totals ranging from 6 to 12 inches occurred over the westernmost counties (west of Kentucky Lake), including the Paducah, Mayfield, and Murray areas. The majority of this rain fell within a 10-hour window between midnight and 10 AM. The highest confirmed rainfall total was 12.76 inches in Graves County, west of Mayfield near the small community of Fancy Farm. The Kentucky mesonet site six miles southwest of Mayfield received 11.28 of rain in a 24-hour period. Preliminary data indicates this broke the previous Kentucky state record for 24-hour rainfall. The old record was 10.48 in Louisville, KY back on March 1, 1997.||In addition to all the flooding, there were several reports of trees blown down across roads. A couple of large hail reports were also received.||The historic rainfall event was caused by a persistent thunderstorm complex that continually regenerated as it moved southeast across the region during the early morning hours of the 19th. This complex of thunderstorms was indirectly caused by the complex of severe thunderstorms during the midday hours of the 18th. The complex on the 18th left an outflow boundary from south central Missouri into northeast Arkansas. This boundary lifted back northeast into southeast Missouri during the overnight and early morning hours of July 19th. At the same time, a southwest low-level jet ramped up over the top of the surface boundary. Extremely high moisture levels were present, with precipitable water values up to 2.3 inches. The position of the boundary oriented parallel with the upper-level wind flow provided an ideal setup for training convection over the same areas. The initial storms blew up by 11 PM and continued to channel southeastward across the same areas through the following morning.
episodes.180969: Major flash flooding struck parts of far southern Illinois. The hardest hit counties were Alexander, Pulaski, and Massac in the southern tip of Illinois. Widespread flash flooding of roads made travel difficult or impossible for several hours during the peak of the heaviest rainfall in the morning. There was a bridge that was washed out in Massac County on a secondary road. Among the most impactful road closures was Interstate 57 in Pulaski County. Illinois Route 3 was closed to most vehicles except large trucks at the underpass on the north side of Cairo. Several water rescues were conducted for people stranded in vehicles in Massac, Pulaski, and Alexander Counties. A number of roads were washed out in several counties. The impacts in the Marion, Carbondale, and Herrin areas consisted of street flooding, as well as some minor flooding of a few structures in flood-prone areas. Widespread rainfall totals ranging from 5 to 9 inches occurred along and south of a line from Carbondale to Marion, including the Cairo and Metropolis areas. The majority of this rain fell within a 10-hour window between midnight and 10 AM. The highest reported rainfall total was 8.68 inches in Ullin (Pulaski County). The co-op site near Cairo received 7.83 of rain.|| The historic rainfall event was caused by a persistent thunderstorm complex that continually regenerated as it moved southeast across the region during the early morning hours of the 19th. This complex of thunderstorms was indirectly caused by the complex of severe thunderstorms during the midday hours of the 18th. The complex on the 18th left an outflow boundary from south central Missouri into northeast Arkansas. This boundary lifted back northeast into southeast Missouri during the overnight and early morning hours of July 19th. At the same time, a southwest low-level jet ramped up over the top of the surface boundary. Extremely high moisture levels were present, with precipitable water values up to 2.3 inches. The position of the boundary oriented parallel with the upper-level wind flow provided an ideal setup for training convection over the same areas. The initial storms blew up by 11 PM and continued to channel southeastward across the same areas through the following morning.
episodes.180970: Cape Girardeau County was on the western edge of a swath of extremely heavy rainfall that caused catastrophic flooding in western Kentucky and the southern tip of Illinois. Rainfall amounts were generally 6 to 12 inches in those areas, but rainfall amounts in Cape Girardeau County were mostly 5 to 6 inches. The historic rainfall event was caused by a persistent thunderstorm complex that continually regenerated as it moved southeast across the region during the early morning hours of the 19th. This complex of thunderstorms was indirectly caused by the complex of severe thunderstorms during the midday hours of the 18th. The complex on the 18th left an outflow boundary from south central Missouri into northeast Arkansas. This boundary lifted back northeast into southeast Missouri during the overnight and early morning hours of July 19th. At the same time, a southwest low level jet ramped up over the top of the surface boundary. Extremely high moisture levels were present, with precipitable water values up to 2.3 inches. The position of the boundary oriented parallel with the upper-level wind flow provided an ideal setup for training convection over the same areas. The initial storms blew up by 11 PM and continued to channel southeastward across the same areas through the following morning.
episodes.181101: Tropical Storm Calvin passed just south of the Big island, and its rain bands with deep convection led to periods of heavy rainfall and minor flooding for portions of the Big Island. The Tropical Storm also brought high winds to portions of the Big Island.
episodes.181211: Preexisting hot and muggy conditions contributed to unsettled weather in West Virginia on both July 17th and 18th. Each afternoon observed strong to severe thunderstorms sprouting during peak heating hours, with damaging winds and a few instances of hails accompanying convection. Tree damage was the primary result of the passing storms, especially across portions of central and southern West Virginia.
episodes.181403: Severe thunderstorms with large hail developed over portions of Platte and Goshen County late in the afternoon on the 19th. One particular left-moving supercell thunderstorm produce very large hail near Torrington damaging numerous cars and home windows.
episodes.181405: Strong to severe thunderstorms moved into the Nebraska Panhandle from eastern Wyoming late in the afternoon on the 19th producing large hail in southern Sioux County.
episodes.181676: Heavy rain from showers and thunderstorms caused flooding and mudslides across central and northern Nevada.
episodes.181917: A heat advisory was in effect for heat index values of 108-112F.  Sea breeze storms across north-central Florida produced localized wet downbursts.
episodes.181941: A couple of thunderstorms produced gale-force wind gusts over the middle tidal Potomac River and central Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.182157: A thunderstorm occasionally became severe as it tracked across portions of southwestern and south central South Dakota. The storm produced large hail and wind gusts to 60 mph.
episodes.182254: Scattered showers and thunderstorms with heavy rainfall developed across the White Mountains and areas northward on the afternoon of the 18th. Moist air supported torrential rainfall rates between 2 to 3 inches an hour, all of which fell over saturated soils. Localized flash flooding resulted where storms trained over the same locations.
episodes.182343: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a boundary that had stalled across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182344: Scattered thunderstorms developed along a boundary that had stalled across the the Ohio Valley.
episodes.182533: Thunderstorms developed during the evening hours ahead of an advancing surface trough where ample moisture was present. Two storms became severe, producing one-inch diameter hail. In addition, one storm produced a funnel cloud in southeastern Wells County.
episodes.182646: A line of thunderstorms passed across Tazewell County during the early morning hours of July 19th, producing anywhere from 1.75 inches to 2.25 inches of rainfall within a hour. Automated rain gages indicated that rainfall rates at times were in excess of 3 inches per hour.  Further east, a thunderstorm over Pittsylvania County produced frequent cloud to ground lightning.  One of these strikes triggered a chimney fire to a house.
episodes.182920: Thunderstorms developed along a cold front brought severe weather to central South Dakota during the evening hours. A storm moved into Pierre and Fort Pierre, SD, producing hail. There were numerous reports of baseball-sized hail across the area, and even one larger than a softball, with an estimated diameter of 5.0 inches. The hailstone is the largest on record in Hughes County (4.0 in Pierre on 6/30/1997 and Blunt on 8/26/2018). Damage was done to vehicles, roofs, and other outside structures. The storm also produced a brief tornado about 11 miles south of Fort Pierre, just west of US Highway 83, around 6:45 pm CDT. These storms then moved south and east through the evening, producing large hail and damaging winds. A wind gust of 100 mph was recorded just west of Oacoma at 8:15 pm CDT via a weather station from the South Dakota State University's mesonet. Damage was done to power poles, trees, trailers, and other property in and around Oacoma.
episodes.182926: A squall line dropped south-southeast from middle Tennessee through north Alabama during the mid to late afternoon hours of the 18th. One brief tornado was spawned along the line in northern Madison County, and numerous other reports of wind damage were received.
episodes.183038: An old thunderstorm complex moving across the area from the prior evening of the 18th entered a more favorable environment by midday and developed a tornado that tracked several miles over the northern Coastal Plain of central NC. Numerous reports of damage to trees and structures confirmed the tornado as it moved from near Nashville, North Carolina to near Battleboro, North Carolina, Continuing northeast to Scotland Neck. The Tornado produced EF3 damage, with up to 150 mph. Additionally, a boundary over the Sandhills to southern Coastal Plain brought several reports of downed trees and powerlines, along with isolated flash flooding in Cumberland County.
episodes.183100: A warm front moved across the Northland during the day on the 19th setting the stage for severe storms during the afternoon and evening across the region. The storms that developed were prolific hail producers with hail to the size of baseballs reported in northern Itasca County. A few isolated reported of tree damage were received, but hail was the primary threat from these storms. Additionally, lightning struck a barn that was over 100 years old starting a fire that completely destroyed the barn.
episodes.183101: A warm front moved across the Northland during the day on the 19th setting the stage for severe storms during the afternoon and evening across the region. The storms that developed were prolific hail producers with hail to the size of limes reported in Burnett and Washburn counties that led to damage. While hail was the primary threat from these storms, one storm did produce a large area of tree damage near Cable with a few other scattered reports of tree damage in the area as well.
episodes.183155: Storms moved through NW MN in the afternoon hours of July 19th. They produced hail up to golf ball sized and a brief touchdown in Beltrami county.
episodes.183237: A modest push of monsoon moisture and ongoing extreme heat fueled spotty thunderstorms over southern Nevada. Isolated high winds and flash flooding occurred.
episodes.183415: A warm, muggy and unstable air mass was in place across eastern Kentucky on July 18th as a wavering front remained northwest of the Lower Ohio River. The first storm cluster of the day fired over central Kentucky during the early afternoon hours before moving into eastern Kentucky. This initial round of storms impacted areas primarily north of the Hal Rogers Parkway during the late afternoon and early evening. The combination of dry air in the mid-levels and sufficient shear led to a a couple of strong bowing line segments with estimated peak wind gusts in the 60 to 70 mph range. The most numerous instances of wind damage, primarily downed trees and power lines, were observed in Estill, Lee, Montgomery and Bath counties. A gust of 61 mph was recorded at the RAWS site close to the Jackson National Weather Service Office. A second larger convective system dropped into the the Commonwealth during the mid-afternoon but then decayed as it moved onto the Cumberland Plateau. However, some cells with this system will still strong enough to bring a few instances of severe wind damage to portions of southcentral Kentucky.
episodes.183463: An isolated supercell initially moved south through the panhandle during the mid and late afternoon hours of July 18, which was responsible for very large hail and some damaging winds. Additional storms developed ahead of that cell toward the Colorado border. A second round of storms, including clusters and a supercell, moved through north central Nebraska shortly after and produced very large hail.
episodes.183479: A shift in the atmospheric pattern from mid to late July brought an array of impacts to much of Utah, including severe thunderstorm wind gusts, large hail, and flash flooding.
episodes.183555: On the evening of July 19th, showers and thunderstorms moved through the far southwestern region of Nebraska. One of the thunderstorms became severe and produced hail up to quarters in size.
episodes.183560: On the evening of July 19th, showers and thunderstorms moved through the northwestern region of Kansas. Some of the thunderstorms became severe and produced hail up to quarters in size along with damaging wind gusts up to an estimated 90 mph.
episodes.183579: A mesoscale convective system moved into the northeast portion of West Tennessee during the early morning hours of July 19, 2023. The environment was favorable for severe hail and damaging winds with about 3000 J/kg of mixed layer convective available potential energy and steep lapse rates. Slow storm motion, training storms, and precipitable water values greater than two inches resulted in some flash flooding.
episodes.183648: Scattered thunderstorms developed across inland portions of southeast South Carolina in the mid afternoon hours near a surface trough. These thunderstorms moved toward the coast and produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183651: Scattered thunderstorms developed across inland portions of southeast Georgia in the early evening hours near a surface trough. These thunderstorms moved toward the coast and produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183779: A severe thunderstorm in Sedgwick County produced quarter size hail near Ovid.
episodes.183814: An outflow boundary from a decaying MCS tracked southward produced a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across the northern portions of Alabama, mainly during the evening hours.
episodes.183822: A few storms developed along a pre-frontal boundary in a zone of weak moisture convergence.  An abundance of dry air above the surface resulted in healthy downdrafts, which produced spotty thunderstorm wind gusts and some stronger non-thunderstorm winds.
episodes.183823: A few storms developed during the afternoon along a cold frontal boundary with up to 2000 J/kg available CAPE and 40 to 50 knots of effective shear.  Rotating storms produced large hail, and isolated very large hail across southwest Minnesota.
episodes.183824: A few storms developed during the afternoon along a cold frontal boundary with up to 2000 J/kg available CAPE and 40 to 50 knots of effective shear. Rotating storms produced large hail, and isolated very large hail across southwest Minnesota.
episodes.183957: Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred oceanside of the Upper Florida Keys as a weak tropical wave passed westward through the Florida Keys and adjacent coastal waters.
episodes.183959: Lightning damaged a dock at Big Coppitt Key as a tropical wave moved west through the Florida Keys, accompanied by scattered thunderstorms.
episodes.183976: Scattered thunderstorms developed over the North Carolina mountains during the afternoon. A couple of these storms produced brief damaging wind gusts. A weakening line of thunderstorms then moved into the mountains from east Tennessee late in the evening. These storms produced additional isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183979: An isolated storm developed over the Blue Ridge mountains and moved southeast into upstate South Carolina during the evening. The storm produced brief damaging wind gusts over northern Pickens County. A cluster of storms later moved into the Upstate from western North Carolina during the early morning hours and produced additional isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.184011: Multiple mesoscale convective systems developed in northwest flow aloft and tracked across the Mid-South. The first tracked from southeast Missouri and southwest Kentucky into West Tennessee during the early-mid afternoon on July 18th. The second mesoscale convective system developed over southern Missouri and tracked across northeast Arkansas, the Memphis metropolitan area, and north Mississippi. These systems were supported by a very moist and unstable airmass with surface-based convective available potential energy values exceeding 6000 J/kg and precipitable water values greater than 2 inches. Adequate amounts of wind shear aloft helped to organize storms as well. Numerous severe storms occurred across the Mid-South with a few reports of large hail and many reports of damaging wind. The Memphis area was among the hardest hit with power outages to over 130,000 utility customers in Shelby County.
episodes.184178: Several supercell thunderstorms developed across the region and produce widespread hail, with occasional strong wind gusts and wind damage.
episodes.184252: A line of thunderstorms passed across Mercer County during the early morning hours of July 19th, producing anywhere from 1.75 inches to 2.25 inches of rainfall within a hour.  Automated rain gages indicated that rainfall rates at times were in excess of 3 inches per hour.
episodes.184289: Persistent southerly flow brought a very moist airmass into the region ahead of a slow moving upper level disturbance and slow moving surface frontal boundary during the afternoon of July 18th.  Storms developed by early afternoon brining isolated areas of wind damage and large hail to both Southern and Northern New Hampshire.
episodes.184304: A few thunderstorms developed and moved through during the evening hours. One such storm became severe and produced damaging winds.
episodes.184325: Several supercell thunderstorms developed across the region and produce widespread hail, with occasional strong wind gusts and wind damage. Of particular note was hail that was 2 to 2.5 inches south of Rice Lake WI.
episodes.184387: An upper level high pressure center was located over central Arizona and central New Mexico which resulted in a favorable pattern for efficient diurnal wind fluctuations including upslope oriented winds towards WFO Pueblo's eastern mountains. Weak waves embedded in the upper level northwesterly flow enhanced the lift and the pattern enhanced the deep shear. The result was a very rare mountainous tornado that was observed at around 9,000 feet.
episodes.184390: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of southeast Virginia.
episodes.184391: Isolated severe thunderstorm associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced damaging winds across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.184392: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced gusty winds across portions of the Chesapeake Bay and Virginia Coastal Waters.
episodes.184393: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced gusty winds across portions of the northeast North Carolina Coastal Waters.
episodes.184394: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced gusty winds across portions of the James River.
episodes.184462: Isolated storms developed across the area, mainly south of I-70. Some of the storms were severe and produced large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.184874: Widespread strong to severe thunderstorms impacted the inland sounds, coastal waters, Pamlico, and Pungo Rivers bringing damaging winds during the evening hours on July 19th.
episodes.185828: Ample mid and upper level moisture that streamed across western Nevada, coupled with summer daytime heating, increased instability across the region that allowed for increased shower and thunderstorm chances (15-30%) that extended mostly south of US-50 from southern Mono County through Mineral counties. These storms were forecast to be a hybrid variety capable of gusty outflow winds up to 50 mph, heavy rainfall, and isolated dry strikes outside of storm cores.

Significant flash flooding occurred in the city of Cape Girardeau. A sport utility vehicle was swept off a roadway and into a creek. The vehicle came to rest against a pile of debris in the creek in Arena Park. The occupants safely escaped with no injuries. Elsewhere in Cape Girardeau, emergency crews responded to a water rescue when a sport utility vehicle became stalled in floodwaters. The driver was safely carried to safety. There was also some flooding in Jackson, but no major impacts were reported there. The co-operative observer at Jackson measured 5.11 inches for the total rainfall on the 18th and 19th. Most of this rainfall occurred during the flash flood on the morning of the 19th.

The remnants of a Mesoscale Convective Vortex initiated a tornadic supercell on its southeastern quadrant as it quickly moved into the northern Coastal Plain early Wednesday morning. The tornado initially touched down southwest of Dortches, NC where power poles were bent and hardwoods snapped at the trunk were observed. The|tornado crossed I-95 just north of exit 138 and produced widespread tree damage on both sides of I-95 and in the median. As it moved into the municipality of Dortches the first instances of EF-2 damage was observed as it entered into a neighborhood |comprised of single-wide units. Multiple single-wide homes were completely destroyed and removed 20-30 yards from their foundation. As the tornado continued along its east-northeast path, a row of 10-15 power poles were snapped and laid out across South Browntown Road, continuing the path of EF-2 damage. Farther to the northeast, the tornado ripped across North Carolina Highway 48 where more power poles were snapped at the base and a residence building suffered major damage as all exterior walls had collapsed with only interior walls and a brick fireplace remained standing. The |tornado then progressed into the Belmont Lake Golf Club where it strengthened into an EF-3 tornado with winds of 140-150 mph. The tornado flattened a metal truss tower connected to the electrical transmission line as well as caused significant damage to a metal warehouse building. Additionally, semi-trucks were flipped and destroyed that where located in a large parking lot near the warehouse.
The tornado then weakened slightly as it crossed into Edgecombe County causing damage to a metal structure before lifting 9 miles east-northeast of Battleboro, NC.
Heavy rain caused flooding in the parking lot of the Hampton Inn in Dickson. No damages are known.

Subsequently, Capitol Reef National Park reported that state Route 24 east of the visitor center was impassable due to high water and debris. Additionally, minor flooding was reported in the campground.
